subject: Ancient History
name: Ancient History, Year 12
about: HSC, Pompeii and Herculaneum, Sparta, Hatshepsut and Augustus
syllabus: NSW Ancient History Stage 6 Syllabus (2017), Year 12 course, the core and one option per section

units.title: Cities of Vesuvius, Pompeii and Herculaneum

points.title: The setting of Pompeii and Herculaneum
points.brief: Two Roman towns on the Bay of Naples, Pompeii a busy trading town and Herculaneum a smaller seaside town, both near Mount Vesuvius.

points.title: The eruption of AD 79
points.brief: Vesuvius buried Pompeii in ash and pumice and Herculaneum in deep pyroclastic flows, which preserved the two towns differently.

points.title: Pliny the Younger's letters
points.brief: Pliny the Younger described the eruption and his uncle's death in two letters to the historian Tacitus, the only eyewitness written account.

points.title: The history of excavation
points.brief: Early digs from the 1700s hunted treasure. Fiorelli in the 1860s began careful records and plaster casts of bodies. Excavation goes on today.

points.title: Human remains as evidence
points.brief: Skeletons found at Herculaneum's boat sheds in the 1980s and 1990s reveal the health, diet and ages of the victims.

points.title: The economy
points.brief: The towns traded wine, garum (fish sauce) and cloth. Shops, bakeries, fulleries and inns show a busy local economy.

points.title: Social structure
points.brief: Society included elite families, freedmen, slaves and women of different ranks. Freedmen could become rich and powerful.

points.title: Local politics
points.brief: Painted election notices on walls show candidates for local offices and who supported them.

points.title: Religion
points.brief: Temples to Roman gods and to the Egyptian goddess Isis, and household shrines called lararia, show public and private worship.

points.title: Houses and daily life
points.brief: Houses such as the House of the Faun show wealth through wall paintings, mosaics and gardens, while graffiti records everyday thoughts.

points.title: Leisure
points.brief: Public baths, theatres and the amphitheatre, the oldest surviving stone one, were centres of social life.

points.title: Conserving the sites
points.brief: Weather, tourism, earlier poor restorations and collapses, such as the House of the Gladiators in 2010, threaten the sites.

points.title: Tourism and the sites
points.brief: Millions visit each year, which pays for conservation but also wears the sites down.

points.title: Changing interpretations
points.brief: New technology and new excavations keep changing what historians think about the towns, such as the date of the eruption.

units.title: Spartan society to the Battle of Leuctra, 371 BC

points.title: The geography of Sparta
points.brief: Sparta lay in the fertile Eurotas valley in Laconia, ringed by mountains, and conquered neighbouring Messenia.

points.title: Spartiates, perioikoi and helots
points.brief: Full citizens (Spartiates) were soldiers. The perioikoi were free non-citizens who traded and crafted. Helots were state-owned serfs who farmed the land.

points.title: The government of Sparta
points.brief: Two kings, a council of elders (the gerousia), five ephors elected each year and an assembly of citizens shared power.

points.title: The agoge
points.brief: Spartan boys left home at seven for a harsh state training in obedience, endurance and fighting.

points.title: Women in Sparta
points.brief: Spartan women exercised, owned land and ran households while men served in the army, giving them more freedom than women in Athens.

points.title: The Spartan army
points.brief: Spartans fought as hoplites in a phalanx, and their discipline made them the most feared soldiers in Greece.

points.title: Fear of helot revolt
points.brief: Spartans, greatly outnumbered by helots, feared revolt, which shaped their military way of life and harsh control.

points.title: Religion and festivals
points.brief: Festivals such as the Karneia and Hyakinthia were central to Spartan life, and Spartans sometimes delayed going to war to complete them.

points.title: The Battle of Leuctra
points.brief: In 371 BC Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra, breaking Spartan military power and soon freeing Messenia.

points.title: Hatshepsut's family background
points.brief: Hatshepsut was the daughter of Thutmose I and wife of Thutmose II, and became regent for the young Thutmose III.

points.title: Becoming pharaoh
points.brief: Within a few years she took the full titles of pharaoh and ruled as co-regent with Thutmose III.

points.title: Claiming legitimacy
points.brief: She used images of herself as a male king and a story of divine birth from the god Amun to support her right to rule.

points.title: Building at Deir el-Bahri
points.brief: Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, with its terraces and reliefs, recorded her achievements and her link to Amun.

points.title: The expedition to Punt
points.brief: Reliefs at Deir el-Bahri show a trading expedition to Punt that brought back incense trees, gold and exotic animals.

points.title: Erasure and evaluation
points.brief: Late in Thutmose III's reign many of her images were destroyed. Historians debate why, and how to judge her reign.

units.title: The Augustan age, 44 BC to AD 14

points.title: Octavian after Caesar's death
points.brief: Named heir in Julius Caesar's will, the young Octavian used Caesar's name and soldiers to win power after 44 BC.

points.title: The Second Triumvirate
points.brief: Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus took power together in 43 BC and defeated Caesar's assassins at Philippi in 42 BC.

points.title: The Battle of Actium
points.brief: In 31 BC Octavian's fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, leaving Octavian sole ruler.

points.title: The settlements of 27 and 23 BC
points.brief: Octavian appeared to restore the Republic and took the name Augustus, while gaining powers that let him control the provinces, the army and the state.

points.title: The powers of Augustus
points.brief: Augustus held tribunician power and command of the armies, and called himself princeps, first citizen, to avoid the title of king.

points.title: Social and moral reform
points.brief: Laws encouraged marriage and children among the upper classes and punished adultery.

points.title: Building and propaganda
points.brief: Monuments such as the Ara Pacis and the Forum of Augustus, coins and poets such as Virgil spread the image of a peaceful golden age.

points.title: The problem of succession
points.brief: Augustus's chosen heirs died one after another, until he adopted Tiberius, who succeeded him in AD 14.

points.title: Evaluating Augustus
points.brief: Ancient writers such as Tacitus and Suetonius judged Augustus differently, and historians debate whether he restored or ended the Republic.
